observation: Start set = \w, but the attempt's first op is \b, so every \w byte inside a word is a full out-of-line call to rx_match_anchored that fails at rx_L0, then the 5-way result-code compare chain and rx_reset_for_next_attempt. On the subjects ~0.77 attempt calls per subject byte, of which ~78% are inner-word positions (avg word 4.4 bytes).
proposed_change: Start positions = WORD STARTS: skip a start byte whose predecessor is \w; after a failed attempt (always at a word start) skip the rest of the word, then the non-\w gap.
regime: sparse-match find-all over word-dense text (all three subjects; ~0.18 calls/byte instead of ~0.77)
correctness_argument: At an inner-word \w byte both sides of \b are \w, so rx_L0 fails before any SET/PUSH: no slot, trail, step or work side effect (fail with resume_depth 0 returns -1 before the step decrement). The \b reads subject[p-1] regardless of search_from, so the filter reads the same byte. match_api: positions a start-set proof excludes consume no budget.

observation: Both spans push a resume frame and give back one byte per backtrack: \w+ (rx_L7) re-runs rx_L5's two trailed SETs and the \b at rx_L3, which can never pass; \s+ (rx_L11) re-runs the backreference at a \s byte, which can never match. ~0.89 backtrack pops per subject byte, each with trail unwind.
proposed_change: Drop RX_PUSH(&&rx_L7) and RX_PUSH(&&rx_L11): the spans become possessive.

correctness_argument: Give-back of \w+ to a shorter length leaves a \w byte on both sides of the following \b (span bytes are \w; the maximal span's next byte is \w only at the window clamp, where every shorter length is also inside the run). Give-back of \s+ puts \1's first byte (group 1 is non-empty, all \w) against a \s byte; ASCII \w and \s are disjoint. So every resumed path fails.
